answer: Under the CPWD contract's arbitration provisions, a claim of about Rs. 18 crore goes to a sole arbitrator: a sole arbitrator applies where the claimed amount is Rs. 20 Crore or less, and a three-arbitrator tribunal applies only where the claimed value is more than Rs. 20 Crore [S1]. Rs. 18 crore is below Rs. 20 Crore, so a sole arbitrator applies [S1]. You cannot go straight to arbitration, because each party invoking arbitration must first exhaust the dispute settlement mechanism [S3]. First, within 15 days of the dispute arising, you must ask the Chief Engineer/CPM, or the ADG/SDG if there is no Chief Engineer/CPM. That officer then refers the disputes to the Dispute Redressal Committee (DRC) within 15 days, together with a list of disputes and amounts claimed [S4]. The DRC gives its decision within 60 days, which can be extended by 30 days with both parties' consent [S4]. The ADG/SDG then has 30 days from receiving the DRC decision to accept it or not [S4]. Lawyers may not represent either party before the DRC [S4]. If you are dissatisfied with the decision, or the time limits run out, you may give notice for appointment of an arbitrator within 30 days, on the proforma in Appendix XVII, and tell the other party [S3]. Your notice must list the disputes with the amount claimed for each and refer to the ADG/SDG decision on the DRC finding [S2]. The CE/ADG/SDG appoints the sole arbitrator within 30 days of receiving the request [S3]. Because the claims exceed Rs. 1,00,000/-, the arbitrator must give reasons for the award [S2]. Note that these rules come from the CPWD contract; if your contract is a different one (for example, the Rajasthan PWD tender), these sources do not cover its arbitration terms.

answer: Under Clause 15 of the CPWD General Conditions of Contract, a suspension ordered for the safety of the works or part thereof is reason (c), which is distinct from suspension caused by the contractor's default under reason (a) [S1]. For reasons (b) and (c), you get an extension of time equal to the period of every such suspension PLUS 25%. This extension applies to completion of the item or group of items of work that has its own completion period in the contract and that includes the suspended work [S1]. You can also recover idle labour costs, but only if the total period of all such suspensions for that item or group of items exceeds thirty days [S2]. In that case you are entitled to such compensation as the Engineer-in-Charge considers reasonable for salaries and/or wages paid to your employees and labour at site who remained idle during the suspension [S2]. A further 2% is added to cover your indirect expenses [S2]. This is conditional on you submitting your claim, supported by details, to the Engineer-in-Charge within fifteen days of the expiry of the period of 30 days [S2]. During the suspension you must properly protect and secure the works and follow the Engineer-in-Charge's instructions [S1]. If the suspension lasts more than three months at a time, you may serve a written notice asking for permission to proceed within fifteen days [S2]. If permission is not granted, you may give written notice treating the suspension as an omission of that part of the works [S2][S7].
